evidence: Cic. Att. 14.18.4: dē Graeciā cotīdiē magis et magis cōgitō (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Phil. 1.5: cum cotīdiē magis magisque perditī hominēs tēctīs ac templīs urbis minārentur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Also magis ac magis, and in verse magis magis (Catullus). Often with cotīdiē or in diēs for growth over time.

terms.grammar: phrase: in with the accusative plural, with a comparative or magis
evidence: Cic. Mil. 25: tantō hic magis in diēs convalēscēbat (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: “More by the day”: in diēs blandius, more seductive every day. Without a comparative in diēs is simply “day by day, daily” (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: dē Graeciā cotīdiē magis et magis cōgitō
phrases.english: every day I think more and more about Greece

phrases.latin: malest, Cornificī, tuō Catullō, malest, mē hercule, et labōriōsē, et magis magis in diēs et hōrās
phrases.english: your Catullus is unwell, Cornificius, unwell, by Hercules, and in pain, and more so every day and hour

phrases.latin: somnus enim et vīnum et epulae … balineaque et ōtium cōnsuētūdine in diēs blandius ita ēnervāvērunt corpora animōsque
phrases.english: for sleep and wine and feasting, baths and idleness, more seductive every day from habit, so weakened their bodies and spirits
